        • Regular elections: second Monday of May unless otherwise provided by law. ‘Unless otherwise provided by law’ means a law fixing another date or delegating it to COMELEC; COMELEC cannot suspend an election on its own (Bañas-Nograles).
        • A district created after the election period has begun applies at the next regular election; resetting the election would give the winner less than the three-year term of Sec. 7 (Bañas-Nograles).
        • Vacancies (Sec. 9): a special election ‘may be called … in the manner prescribed by law’; the winner serves only the unexpired term. Senate: with the next regular election (Tolentino, 2004). House: COMELEC must call it 60 to 90 days after the vacancy (if at least one year remains) without waiting for a House resolution (Hagedorn, 2025).
        • Mandamus lies against COMELEC but not the House: Sec. 9 says ‘may’, so a House resolution is discretionary; RA 7166 deleted RA 6645’s certification requirement and changed the reckoning to one year before the term expires. COMELEC may rely on official press releases or a certification from the Speaker or Secretary-General (Hagedorn).

        Last-minute checklist

        • Qualifications table; they cannot be added by law (SJS v. DDB).
        • Atong Paglaum’s parameters; Albano (Congress can legislate, but rationally); Duterte Youth (substitution deadlines; voters’ right to know nominees).
        • COMELEC (group, nominations) versus HRET (sitting member).
        • Seat formula: 2%, guaranteed seat, proportional additional seats, cap of 3; divisor per Araro.
        • Special elections: Senate with next regular election; House 60 to 90 days, COMELEC calls (Hagedorn).
        • Second-placer rule abandoned (Mangudadatu).

        Congress: officers, quorum, rules, discipline and the Journal

        Syllabus V.A.3: Art. VI, Secs. 15 and 16; 16 cases. Tested in 2023 (Teves expulsion), 2013 (counting a hospitalized member for quorum), 2015 finals (absentee members and the Ombudsman).

        The provisions

        Art. VI, Sec. 16(1) The Senate shall elect its President and the House of Representatives, its Speaker, by a majority vote of all its respective Members. Each House shall choose such other officers as it may deem necessary.
        (2) A majority of each House shall constitute a quorum to do business, but a smaller number may adjourn from day to day and may compel the attendance of absent Members in such manner, and under such penalties, as such House may provide.
        (3) Each House may determine the rules of its proceedings, punish its Members for disorderly behavior, and, with the concurrence of two-thirds of all its Members, suspend or expel a Member. A penalty of suspension, when imposed, shall not exceed sixty days.
        (4) Each House shall keep a Journal of its proceedings, and from time to time publish the same, excepting such parts as may, in its judgment, affect national security; and the yeas and nays on any question shall, at the request of one-fifth of the Members present, be entered in the Journal. Each House shall also keep a Record of its proceedings.
        (5) Neither House during the sessions of the Congress shall, without the consent of the other, adjourn for more than three days, nor to any other place than that in which the two Houses shall be sitting.

        Officers and internal rules

        • Only the Senate President and Speaker are constitutionally elected (majority of all Members). Everything else (minority leader, committee chairs) is for the chamber (Santiago v. Guingona; Baguilat).
        • Courts do not enforce purely internal rules (Arroyo v. De Venecia), except when (a) a constitutional requirement is involved (quorum, voting, publication: Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole), or (b) third parties’ rights are affected (Pacete).
        • In Pacete, a member’s motion to reconsider a confirmation, never acted on, did not undo it: only a majority of the Commission’s members present can reopen and recall a confirmation. A single member cannot act for the body.

        Quorum

        A majority of the members within the coercive jurisdiction of the chamber (Avelino v. Cuenco: 12 of 23 senators present in the country). Quorum is presumed to continue unless challenged through the chamber’s procedure; the Journal and the enrolled bill control (Tinio v. Duterte, 2023).

        • Avelino arithmetic: 12 is half of 24 and not a majority; it was a quorum only because one senator was abroad, leaving a base of 23. Absent members within the country still count in the base, and a smaller number may compel their attendance (Sec. 16(2)).
        • Quorum is not the vote to elect: under the 1987 Constitution the Senate President and Speaker need a majority of all Members (Sec. 16(1)), which the 1935 text did not require.
        2013 midterm (Dimaporo in hospital detention): he remains a Member and is counted in the base for computing the majority of the House; whether he is ‘present’ for quorum is a different question. Members cannot be compelled to attend while lawfully detained (Jalosjos). Read the question’s exact verb (‘counted as a member’ versus ‘counted as present’).
        In a news question (2015 finals: Ombudsman asked to compel absent members to attend): Sec. 16(2) gives each House the power to compel attendance of absent members ‘in such manner, and under such penalties, as such House may provide’. The remedy is internal. The Ombudsman cannot intrude into a constitutional function of Congress; separation of powers. Members’ salaries are fixed by law, so absence alone does not create a disallowance unless a rule provides a penalty.

        Discipline of members

        Valid suspension or expulsion
        1. Ground: disorderly behavior, as the House determines (wide deference: Osmeña v. Pendatun).
        2. Vote: two-thirds of all Members (not just those present).
        3. Suspension: not more than 60 days. Expulsion has no cap but is the gravest penalty.
        4. Due process: notice and a chance to be heard (Pimentel v. Senate Committee of the Whole).
        5. No conviction required; it is distinct from criminal liability.
        • Alejandrino (1924): courts would not order reinstatement of a suspended senator (decided before the 60-day cap).
        • The Alejandrino majority conceded that a one-year suspension of an appointive senator was a qualified expulsion beyond the Senate’s power, but held it had no power to coerce the Senate. Johnson dissented: the Court may rule on positive acts of another branch that deprive a person of rights. Possibly bad law: no appointive legislators remain, and expanded judicial review now reaches grave abuse by Congress.
        • Osmeña (1960): the speech privilege does not shield a member from his own House; taking up other business does not waive discipline.
        • Osmeña was suspended for 15 months under the 1935 Constitution, which mentioned only expulsion and had no cap: the power to suspend is an inherent legislative prerogative. The 1987 text now caps suspension at 60 days.
        • De Venecia v. Sandiganbayan (2002): a court’s preventive suspension under RA 3019 is not discipline and is valid.
        • De Venecia involved Rep. Ceferino Paredes, Jr. and follows Santiago v. Sandiganbayan (2001), which upheld a 90-day preventive suspension of Senator Defensor Santiago: suspension under Sec. 13 of RA 3019 is mandatory once a valid information is filed, and precautionary, not punitive. The two-thirds vote and 60-day cap do not apply to it.
        • Pobre v. Defensor-Santiago (2009): discipline for floor speech belongs to the chamber, not the courts.
        • Lesser penalties (censure, reprimand, deletion of unparliamentary remarks from the record, fine) are within the general power to ‘punish’ for disorderly behavior; only suspension and expulsion need two-thirds of all Members.
        In a news question (2023 Q1, Teves): no conviction is needed and the Court defers on what is disorderly. But you can argue for him: (1) the House already suspended him twice for 60 days for the same absence, so expelling him for it evades the cap and punishes twice; (2) grounds like a terrorist designation by the Executive and a personal video are not disorderly behavior as a Member; (3) due process. Know both sides.

        Journal, Record and the enrolled bill

        RuleContentCase
        Enrolled bill doctrineThe signatures of the Senate President and Speaker and the secretaries’ certification are conclusive of due enactmentCoTeSCUP (2018); Tinio (2023); Arroyo v. De Venecia
        Probative value of the JournalConclusive on what it records; no extrinsic evidenceU.S. v. Pons
        Journal over enrolled billOnly for matters the Constitution requires in the Journal (yeas and nays on third reading and on veto override, veto messages, yeas and nays on request of one-fifth)Morales v. Subido
        ExceptionIf the presiding officers withdraw their signatures because the enrolled text is wrong, there is no enrolled bill; consult the JournalAstorga v. Villegas
        • Matters the Constitution requires in the Journal: yeas and nays on third reading (Art. VI, Sec. 26(2)); the veto message and the yeas and nays on overriding a veto (Sec. 27(1)); yeas and nays on any question at the request of one-fifth of those present (Sec. 16(4)); and each Member’s vote on impeachment (Art. XI, Sec. 3(3)). Only parts affecting national security may be withheld from publication.
        • The enrolled bill doctrine is court-made, grounded on respect for a coequal branch; the Journal is conclusive on what it records, and courts take judicial notice of it rather than receive extrinsic evidence (Pons).

        Sessions: regular session from the fourth Monday of July until 30 days before the next opening (Sec. 15); the President may call special sessions; joint sessions for war, canvassing presidential votes, martial law revocation or extension, and the SONA.

        Last-minute checklist

        • Speaker and Senate President: majority of all Members; other officers per chamber rules.
        • Quorum: majority within coercive jurisdiction (Avelino); presumed to continue (Tinio).
        • Discipline: disorderly behavior; two-thirds of all Members; suspension max 60 days; no conviction needed.
        • Internal rules not enforced by courts, except constitutional requirements or third-party rights.
        • Enrolled bill conclusive; Astorga exception; Journal for constitutionally required entries.

        Congress: salaries, privileges and disqualifications

        Syllabus V.A.4: Art. VI, Secs. 10 to 14; RA 10530; 11 cases. Tested in 2024 (Liban and RA 10530) and 2013 (arrest of a congressman).

        The provisions

        Art. VI, Secs. 10, 11, 13, 14Section 10. The salaries of Senators and Members of the House of Representatives shall be determined by law. No increase in said compensation shall take effect until after the expiration of the full term of all the Members of the Senate and the House of Representatives approving such increase.
        Section 11. A Senator or Member of the House of Representatives shall, in all offenses punishable by not more than six years imprisonment, be privileged from arrest while the Congress is in session. No Member shall be questioned nor be held liable in any other place for any speech or debate in the Congress or in any committee thereof.
        Section 13. No Senator or Member of the House of Representatives may hold any other office or employment in the Government, or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including government-owned or controlled corporations or their subsidiaries, during his term without forfeiting his seat. Neither shall he be appointed to any office which may have been created or the emoluments thereof increased during the term for which he was elected.
        Section 14. No Senator or Member of the House of Representatives may personally appear as counsel before any court of justice or before the Electoral Tribunals, or quasi-judicial and other administrative bodies. Neither shall he, directly or indirectly, be interested financially in any contract with, or in any franchise or special privilege granted by the Government, or any subdivision, agency, or instrumentality thereof, including any government-owned or controlled corporation, or its subsidiary, during his term of office. He shall not intervene in any matter before any office of the Government for his pecuniary benefit or where he may be called upon to act on account of his office.

        Salaries

        An increase takes effect only after the full term of all members of both Houses who approved it has expired (PHILCONSA v. Mathay). It cannot be achieved indirectly through retirement benefits (Ligot v. Mathay).

        • ‘All the Members’ of both chambers who approved the raise: in PHILCONSA the RA 4134 increase could not take effect before December 30, 1969, when the last senators who voted for it finished their terms. The delay deters legislators from voting themselves raises.
        • A retirement gratuity is compensation; computing it on a raise the member could not receive is an indirect increase (Ligot).

        Freedom from arrest

        Privilege applies only if
        1. the offense is punishable by not more than six years’ imprisonment; and
        2. Congress is in session (regular or special, not recess).
        It does not cover offenses punishable by more than six years, and it never exempts a convicted or lawfully detained member (Jalosjos; Trillanes v. Pimentel).
        • History (Jalosjos): 1935, all offenses except treason, felony and breach of the peace, during attendance at sessions; 1973, offenses punishable by not more than six years, during attendance, with the Batasan bound to surrender the member within 24 hours after adjournment; 1987, offenses punishable by not more than six years, while Congress is in session (attendance not required).
        • Election does not free a detained member: voters knew of his confinement; temporary leave is only for emergencies; detention prisoners, like convicts, cannot hold office while detained (People v. Maceda), and high office is not a substantial distinction for equal protection (Jalosjos; Trillanes).
        2013 midterm (Dimaporo, malversation punishable by more than 6 years, arrested in hospital): the arrest is legal; the privilege covers only offenses punishable by not more than six years. A detained member may be counted in computing the House’s membership but cannot insist on attending sessions (Jalosjos).

        Speech and debate

        The privilege covers utterances and acts in the performance of legislative functions: floor speeches, votes, bills, committee proceedings (Jimenez v. Cabangbang). It does not cover press releases, open letters or media interviews (Jimenez; Trillanes v. Castillo-Marigomen). It protects against being questioned ‘in any other place’, not against the member’s own chamber (Osmeña) or against the chamber’s discipline (Pobre).

        • Protected acts (Jimenez): (1) floor speeches while in session; (2) statements made or votes cast in the halls of Congress while in session; (3) bills introduced, whether in session or not; (4) other official acts, inside or outside Congress, in the discharge of legislative or committee duties.
        • The privilege attaches because the statement furthers legislation, not because a lawmaker made it; press statements are ‘political in nature, rather than legislative’ (Trillanes v. Castillo-Marigomen). Its purpose is to let members speak with the fullest liberty, free from the resentment of the powerful (Osmeña).

        Incompatible and forbidden offices

        Incompatible office (first sentence)Forbidden office (second sentence)
        Which officesAny other office or employment in the government, its subdivisions, agencies, instrumentalities, GOCCs and subsidiariesAny office created, or whose emoluments were increased, during the term for which he was elected
        EffectHe may accept, but forfeits his seat (Adaza)He cannot be appointed at all during that term, even if he resigns
        • Adaza applied the 1973 rule (Art. VIII, Sec. 10, as amended), whose only exceptions were Prime Minister and Cabinet member; the 1987 Constitution has no Cabinet exception. Taking the legislative oath vacated the governorship.
        • Do not confuse Art. IX-B, Sec. 7 (no elective official is eligible for appointment to any public office during his tenure; resigning after the appointment does not cure it, Flores v. Drilon) with Art. VI, Sec. 13, under which a legislator may accept another office but forfeits his seat.

        Liban v. Gordon: the PNRC chairmanship is not a government office (the PNRC is sui generis, an auxiliary of government, not a GOCC), so a senator who chairs it keeps his seat. The 2009 ruling that RA 95 was unconstitutional (Congress cannot create a private corporation by special charter, Art. XII, Sec. 16) was reversed in 2011 because it was not the lis mota and the PNRC is not an ordinary private corporation.

        • The test in Liban: the PNRC Chairman is elected by a private-sector-controlled Board and is appointed by neither the President nor a department head, so he is not a government official or employee.
        2024 Q4: how RA 10530 answers Liban. Liban raised: (1) is the PNRC a GOCC (so a legislator chairing it forfeits his seat)? (2) can Congress create the PNRC by special charter when Art. XII, Sec. 16 bars special charters for private corporations? RA 10530 (2013) settles both by statute: it recognizes the PNRC as an independent, autonomous, non-governmental organization auxiliary to the authorities of the Government in the humanitarian field, consistent with the Geneva Conventions. It is neither a GOCC nor a private corporation formed for profit, so (1) its chairmanship is not a government office under Sec. 13, and (2) its charter is not barred by Art. XII, Sec. 16. Mention that the 2011 Resolution had already called the PNRC sui generis; RA 10530 codifies it.

        Sec. 14: no personal appearance as counsel before courts, tribunals or administrative bodies; this cannot be evaded by buying shares to intervene as a ‘stockholder’ (Puyat v. De Guzman). A detained senator-petitioner’s request to argue her own case was denied (Pangilinan v. Cayetano, Notice, 2018).

        • In Puyat, a stockholder intervening for his own interest is ordinarily not appearing as counsel; the token ten shares, bought after his appearance as counsel was objected to, showed an indirect appearance.
        • De Lima asked to appear as a party, not as counsel, so Sec. 14 was not the ground; the denial rested on her detention, and her co-petitioners could argue the case.

        Sec. 12 (disclosure of financial interests and conflicts of interest) and Sec. 20 (COA audit of Congress’s books, with an annual itemized list of amounts paid to each Member) complete the accountability provisions.

        Last-minute checklist

        • Salary increase: after the full term of all members of both Houses who approved it.
        • Arrest privilege: offenses up to 6 years, while in session; not for detention after charge for graver crimes or conviction.
        • Speech: legislative acts only; not media; not immunity from one’s own chamber.
        • Incompatible (forfeits seat) versus forbidden (cannot be appointed) offices.
        • Liban 2009 and 2011; RA 10530: PNRC is independent, autonomous, non-governmental, auxiliary to government.

        Electoral tribunals and the Commission on Appointments

        Syllabus V.A.5–6: Art. VI, Secs. 17 to 19; 12 cases. Tested in 2013 (Muhlach v. Fuentebella: COMELEC or HRET?) and 2015 (Poe: forum).

        The provisions

        Art. VI, Secs. 17 and 18Section 17. The Senate and the House of Representatives shall each have an Electoral Tribunal which shall be the sole judge of all contests relating to the election, returns, and qualifications of their respective Members. Each Electoral Tribunal shall be composed of nine Members, three of whom shall be Justices of the Supreme Court to be designated by the Chief Justice, and the remaining six shall be Members of the Senate or the House of Representatives, as the case may be, who shall be chosen on the basis of proportional representation from the political parties and the parties or organizations registered under the party-list system represented therein. The senior Justice in the Electoral Tribunal shall be its Chairman.
        Section 18. There shall be a Commission on Appointments consisting of the President of the Senate, as ex officio Chairman, twelve Senators, and twelve Members of the House of Representatives, elected by each House on the basis of proportional representation from the political parties and parties or organizations registered under the party-list system represented therein. The chairman of the Commission shall not vote, except in case of a tie. The Commission shall act on all appointments submitted to it within thirty session days of the Congress from their submission. The Commission shall rule by a majority vote of all the Members.

        When does the tribunal take over from COMELEC?

        HRET or SET jurisdiction begins when three things concur (Reyes v. COMELEC, 2013)
        1. A valid proclamation;
        2. a proper oath (for the House, before the Speaker in open session);
        3. assumption of office (on June 30).
        Before that, COMELEC keeps jurisdiction over the winner’s qualifications. If COMELEC’s ruling on the proclamation itself is still pending, the tribunal does not acquire jurisdiction (Codilla). If the COC was finally cancelled before the election, there is no ‘member’ for the tribunal to judge (Velasco).
        • A timely motion for reconsideration suspends a COMELEC Division’s ruling, so a proclamation made under it is premature, and one made without notice and hearing is void; the tribunal cannot take over, since it has no power to review COMELEC rulings (Codilla).
        • Once the COMELEC or Supreme Court ruling is final, the Speaker’s administration of the oath and the Secretary-General’s entry in the Roll of Members are ministerial, so mandamus lies (Codilla; Velasco). Second placer: votes for a candidate not yet disqualified by final judgment are not stray (Codilla), but votes for a candidate whose COC was cancelled as void are, so the qualified candidate with the most valid votes wins (Velasco).
        2013 midterm (Muhlach v. Fuentebella): Fuentebella had been proclaimed; Muhlach’s remedy is an election protest in the HRET once Fuentebella becomes a member (proclamation, oath, assumption). Before assumption, Reyes v. COMELEC says COMELEC still has jurisdiction, so read the dates. The circulated key chose the HRET.

        Nature of the tribunals

        • ‘Sole judge’: independent of the chamber and of the courts; non-partisan (‘a non-political body in a sea of politicians’, Gatmaytan’s book).
        • Members have security of tenure; a chamber cannot remove a member for voting against his party (Bondoc v. Pineda). Valid causes: end of term, death or disability, resignation from the party he represents, formal affiliation with another party, removal for other valid cause.
        • All members must sit; the Justices alone cannot decide (Abbas). A rule requiring at least one Justice for a quorum is valid (Reyes v. HRET).
        • The Supreme Court reviews tribunal decisions only for grave abuse (e.g., annulling precincts without substantial evidence: Abayon).
        • Each chamber chooses its members of the tribunal and the CA; claimants go to the chamber first (Pimentel v. HRET).
        • Annulment of elections versus failure of elections: the tribunal’s annulment is judicial, limited to the precincts in the contest and done only to find who got the majority of legal votes, and no special election follows; COMELEC’s declaration of a failure of elections is administrative and is followed by special elections (Abayon).
        • If inhibitions break the quorum (which needs at least one Justice), the Supreme Court and the House may designate special members (Reyes v. HRET).
        • Party-list: once the group is proclaimed and the nominee takes the oath and assumes office, questions on the member’s qualifications (including expulsion from the group) go to the HRET (Lico; Abayon v. HRET, 2010); registration and cancellation of the group stay with COMELEC (An Waray).

        Commission on Appointments

        Proportional representation in the CA
        1. Senate seats per party = (party’s senators ÷ 24) × 12; House seats computed the same way on the House membership.
        2. Fractions cannot be rounded up at another party’s expense (Guingona v. Gonzales); the CA can function with fewer than 12 from a chamber.
        3. A party must be big enough for at least one seat; being ‘minority’ is not enough (Coseteng).
        4. Thresholds: a party needs at least two senators for one Senate seat, so a lone senator’s 0.5 cannot be rounded up (Guingona); in the House it needs about one-twelfth of the membership (some 17 members in Coseteng), and endorsements from members of other parties do not count. The rule is mandatory, and the composition of the CA is a justiciable question (Guingona; Daza).
        5. Membership may be changed when political alignments change permanently (Daza v. Singson), not for temporary alliances.
        6. Challengers must have standing and first raise the matter in the chamber (Drilon v. De Venecia).

        The CA confirms the appointments listed in Art. VII, Sec. 16 (department heads; ambassadors, public ministers and consuls; officers of the armed forces from colonel or naval captain; other officers whose appointments are vested in the President by the Constitution). Congress cannot add offices requiring confirmation by statute (a structural point that also appears in the finals coverage).

        • The CA and the tribunals must be constituted within 30 days after each chamber organizes (Sec. 19). The CA meets only while Congress is in session, at the call of its Chairman or a majority of all its members, and its power is exercised by the CA as a body, not by individual members.
        • Appointments made while Congress is not in session are effective only until disapproved by the CA or until the next adjournment of Congress (Art. VII, Sec. 16).

        Last-minute checklist

        • Tribunal: 3 Justices + 6 members; senior Justice chairs; ‘sole judge’ of election, returns and qualifications.
        • Jurisdiction: proclamation + oath + assumption (Reyes v. COMELEC).
        • Bondoc: no removal for party disloyalty. Abbas: all must sit. Abayon: grave abuse review.
        • CA: Senate President + 12 + 12; chair votes only to break ties; acts within 30 session days; majority of all Members.
        • Guingona: no rounding up fractions; Daza: permanent realignments; Coseteng: minority status alone gives no seat.

        Powers of Congress, its limits, delegation, and titles of bills

        Syllabus V.A.7 and V.A.8(a)(1): plenary power; substantive limits (P&S 31–37); procedural limits (ABAKADA); titles of bills; plus delegation and the publication of IRRs, which past midterms test heavily (2023 oversight committee; 2024 Bulacan IRR; 2020 finals on IRRs). 9 cases.

        Plenary legislative power

        Art. VI, Sec. 1The legislative power shall be vested in the Congress of the Philippines which shall consist of a Senate and a House of Representatives, except to the extent reserved to the people by the provision on initiative and referendum.

        The grant is broad and plenary: Congress may legislate on any matter of common interest unless the Constitution forbids it or lodges the power elsewhere (Torralba: creating municipalities). Only Congress may create legislative districts, and so provinces and cities (Sema). Congress also has plenary power over election schedules, subject to suffrage and due process (Macalintal, 2023).

        • Sema: the Constitution gives autonomous regions no power to create districts (expressio unius), and a creature of Congress cannot change Congress’s own composition. The ARMM may still create municipalities and barangays, which do not create districts; COMELEC’s resolution keeping the existing district was valid.
        • Torralba: where the Constitution requires a Local Government Code to fix criteria, creations must meet them once the Code exists; before then the legislature’s power stays plenary, subject only to a plebiscite in the units affected.

        Substantive limits (Gatmaytan, P&S)

        1. Unconstitutional laws. Congress cannot pass laws beyond its power, that infringe constitutional principles, or whose purpose or effect violates the Constitution. Courts presume constitutionality and strike down only on a clear breach.
        2. Supermajority votes. Congress cannot require a higher vote to amend or repeal a law; each House passes bills by majority with a quorum. One Congress cannot bind the next.
        3. Irrepealable laws. No law can be made beyond repeal; this would deprive later legislatures of their power.
        4. Retroactive laws. Laws are generally prospective; procedural laws may apply to pending cases; ex post facto laws and bills of attainder are prohibited (Art. III, Sec. 22).
        5. The Supreme Court’s autonomy. Congress cannot exempt anyone from court fees (fiscal autonomy) or alter rules of procedure (Art. VIII, Sec. 5(5)); it cannot increase the Court’s appellate jurisdiction without its advice and concurrence (Art. VI, Sec. 30).
        6. Other express limits: the Bill of Rights; no adding qualifications to constitutional offices (SJS v. DDB); no titles of nobility (Sec. 31); no interpreting the Constitution by statute (Endencia); the money provisions (Secs. 24 to 29).
        7. Others on the class reviewer’s list: riders (Sec. 25(2) for the budget; Sec. 26(1) generally); no amendment on third reading (Sec. 26(2)), though the bicameral conference committee may still reconcile versions; uniform and equitable taxation (Sec. 28(1)); the Court’s advice and concurrence for added appellate jurisdiction (Sec. 30); sunset clauses. If only parts of a law are void, the rest stands unless the parts are so dependent on each other that the legislature meant them as a whole.
        Gatmaytan: his book lists these five substantive limitations (unconstitutional laws, supermajority votes, irrepealable laws, laws with retroactive effect, fiscal autonomy of the Court). When a question involves a law that ‘cannot be amended except by three-fourths’ or ‘shall not be repealed’, cite this list.

        Procedural limits: the legislative veto (ABAKADA)

        After enactment, Congress may only scrutinize (budget hearings, question hour, confirmation) and investigate (inquiries in aid of legislation). It may not supervise. Any law that lets Congress, a committee, or individual members approve, disapprove, or take part in the implementation of a law violates separation of powers, and also bicameralism and presentment, because it lets Congress act with the force of law without passing a bill (ABAKADA). The same reasoning killed the pork barrel (Belgica) and the JCOC over COMELEC’s rules (Macalintal, 2003).

        ABAKADA’s three forms of oversight: scrutiny (requests for reports and information, budget hearings, question hour, confirmation), investigation (a more intense digging of facts, in aid of legislation), and supervision (a continuing and informed awareness of executive operations). Only the first two survive enactment; supervision becomes a legislative veto when Congress keeps a right to approve or disapprove a regulation before it takes effect.

        Is the oversight committee valid?
        1. Does it only review, monitor, require reports, hold hearings and recommend legislation? Valid (scrutiny and investigation).
        2. Does it approve rules, budgets of an agency, or projects; deputize or direct executive agencies; or otherwise take part in enforcement? Invalid (legislative veto or execution by Congress).
        3. Save the rest of the law if separable (ABAKADA kept RA 9335 except Sec. 12).
        2023 Q3 (Tax Code Sec. 290-A, Joint Congressional Oversight Committee on Illicit Trade): reviewing BIR and BOC performance, requiring reports, holding hearings and recommending remedial legislation are valid oversight (scrutiny and investigation in aid of legislation). But the power to deputize the BIR, BOC, PNP and NBI ‘in undertaking its duties’ lets Congress direct law enforcement: execution belongs to the President (Art. VII, Sec. 17). That clause is void under ABAKADA; the rest may stand. Also: ‘in aid of legislation’ cannot cure an executive role.

        Delegation of legislative power

        Potestas delegata non delegari potest. Congress cannot delegate the power to make the law (to decide what the law shall be), but may confer discretion in its execution.

        Valid delegation (both tests)
        1. Completeness: the law sets forth the policy to be executed, leaving nothing for the delegate to decide but how to carry it out.
        2. Sufficient standard: the law fixes limits that are sufficiently determinate or determinable, to which the delegate must conform (e.g., ‘public interest’, ‘reasonable’, ‘just and equitable’ have been accepted when read with the law’s policy).
        Permitted delegations: (1) tariff powers to the President (Art. VI, Sec. 28(2)); (2) emergency powers to the President (Sec. 23(2)); (3) to the people (initiative and referendum); (4) to local governments; (5) to administrative agencies (subordinate legislation).
        • Undue delegation: People v. Vera (provincial boards deciding whether the Probation Act applies). Subdelegation by an agency to private parties is invalid (KMU: operators setting their own fares).
        • Valid: Agustin v. Edu; Zabal (proclamation as subordinate legislation under disaster laws); Garcia v. Executive Secretary (tariffs).
        Valid IRR (Gatmaytan’s book, citing Lokin)
        1. Its promulgation is authorized by the legislature;
        2. it is within the scope of the authority given;
        3. it is promulgated in accordance with the prescribed procedure; and
        4. it is reasonable (germane to the law and consistent with its standards).
        An IRR cannot amend, expand or contradict the law it implements.

        Publication and effectivity

        Laws take effect 15 days after publication in the Official Gazette or a newspaper of general circulation, unless the law provides otherwise (Civil Code, Art. 2 as amended by EO 200). ‘Unless otherwise provided’ refers to the date, not to dispensing with publication: all statutes, including those of local application, and all rules that implement laws must be published (Tañada v. Tuvera, 1985 and 1986). Interpretative rules, purely internal rules, and letters of instruction to subordinates need not be published. Under the Administrative Code (Book VII), agencies must also file rules with the University of the Philippines Law Center (ONAR); rules take effect 15 days after filing unless a different date is fixed.

        2024 Q3 (Bulacan Freeport Act, Sec. 29: DTI to issue IRR within 90 days, in consultation with DOF, NEDA, the Province and a representative of the airport project; effective 15 days after publication in a newspaper of general circulation): (1) No legislative veto: Congress has no role after enactment, unlike ABAKADA. (2) Consultation with a private project representative is not a delegation of rule-making to a private party; the DTI alone promulgates, but it must not let the private developer dictate (KMU). (3) The 90-day period is directory; a late IRR is not void. (4) Publication in one newspaper of general circulation satisfies Tañada and EO 200, but the IRR must also be filed with ONAR under the Administrative Code to bind the public. (5) The law itself must supply the policy and standards (completeness and sufficient standard). Conclusion: Sec. 29 is valid.

        Title and one subject (Art. VI, Sec. 26(1))

        Art. VI, Sec. 26(1)Every bill passed by the Congress shall embrace only one subject which shall be expressed in the title thereof.

        Two purposes (Lidasan): to prevent hodgepodge or log-rolling legislation, and to inform legislators and the public of the bill’s subject so there is no surprise or fraud. Construed liberally: the title need not catalogue every provision; it is enough that it is comprehensive enough to include the general object, and that all provisions are germane to it (Giron). A misleading title voids the law, wholly if the parts are inseparable (Lidasan). A title also limits how far an enabling law can be read (Cruz v. Paras).

        • A title is defective if it misleads, is too restrictive, or omits essential matters in the law; it must lead readers to inquire into the body (Lidasan).
        • Short title versus long title (class reviewer’s Q&A, citing the Bayanihan to Heal as One Act): a longer title cannot cure a defect in the short title, because legislators and the public know the bill by its short name. Use with care: the Court reads the full title (in Giron it relied on RA 9006’s long title, not ‘Fair Election Act’).
        2015 midterm (anti-dynasty rule in the SK Reform Act): the SK law’s title concerns the SK’s structure and eligibility; a rule on SK officials’ relatives is germane to eligibility for SK office, so it is not a rider and does not violate the one-subject rule. Since SK office is statutory, adding qualifications is valid (the ‘adding qualifications’ bar applies to offices whose qualifications the Constitution fixes). The key marked ‘valid’.

        Last-minute checklist

        • Plenary power, except as limited; only Congress creates districts (Sema).
        • Five substantive limits from P&S; plus no added qualifications; no interpreting the Constitution.
        • Post-enactment: scrutiny and investigation only; no approval or execution role (ABAKADA).
        • Delegation: completeness plus sufficient standard; five permitted delegations; no subdelegation.
        • IRR: authorized, within scope, proper procedure, reasonable; published; filed with ONAR.
        • Title rule: no hodgepodge, no surprise; liberal construction; germaneness.

        Appropriation and tax laws

        Syllabus V.A.8(a)(2): appropriation laws (Demetria to Madera) and tax laws (Tolentino to John Hay). 16 cases. Tested in 2013 (DAP-type realignment; PDAF veto), 2015 (GAA after Belgica and Araullo; tax bill origin), 2016 (confidential and intelligence funds), 2020 finals (PAO forensic lab rider).

        The provisions

        Art. VI, Secs. 24, 25(1), 25(2), 25(5), 25(7), 29(1)Section 24. All appropriation, revenue or tariff bills, bills authorizing increase of the public debt, bills of local application, and private bills, shall originate exclusively in the House of Representatives, but the Senate may propose or concur with amendments.
        Section 25. (1) The Congress may not increase the appropriations recommended by the President for the operation of the Government as specified in the budget. The form, content, and manner of preparation of the budget shall be prescribed by law. (2) No provision or enactment shall be embraced in the general appropriations bill unless it relates specifically to some particular appropriation therein. Any such provision or enactment shall be limited in its operation to the appropriation to which it relates. … (5) No law shall be passed authorizing any transfer of appropriations; however, the President, the President of the Senate, the Speaker of the House of Representatives, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court, and the heads of Constitutional Commissions may, by law, be authorized to augment any item in the general appropriations law for their respective offices from savings in other items of their respective appropriations. … (7) If, by the end of any fiscal year, the Congress shall have failed to pass the general appropriations bill for the ensuing fiscal year, the general appropriations law for the preceding fiscal year shall be deemed re-enacted and shall remain in force and effect until the general appropriations bill is passed by the Congress.
        Section 29. (1) No money shall be paid out of the Treasury except in pursuance of an appropriation made by law.

        Other limits: Sec. 25(3) (Congress’s own appropriations follow the same procedure), 25(4) (special appropriations must specify the purpose and be supported by funds actually available), 25(6) (discretionary funds only for public purposes, with vouchers and guidelines), 29(2) (no public money for any church or religious dignitary, with listed exceptions), 29(3) (taxes for a special purpose form a special fund), and the item veto (Sec. 27(2)).

        • What counts as an appropriation: a bill whose primary aim is to set apart public money; a bill creating an office and funding it is not an appropriation bill. An appropriation ‘made by law’ need not be in the GAA: a law setting apart a determinate or determinable amount for a stated purpose suffices, so continuing appropriations (debt service; the Malampaya Fund) need no yearly re-enactment (Guingona v. Carague; Belgica).
        • Public purpose: appropriations must be for a public purpose; Sec. 29(2) bars funds for any religion, but a valid secular purpose that incidentally benefits a religion is allowed.

        The pork barrel line: how doctrine changed

        1. Philconsa v. Enriquez (1994): Countrywide Development Fund upheld (legislators only recommend). Inappropriate provisions may be vetoed separately; conditions cannot be vetoed without the item.
        2. LAMP (2012): PDAF upheld on the same premise.
        3. Belgica (2013): reversal. The PDAF and similar post-enactment powers of legislators are unconstitutional (separation of powers, non-delegation, checks and balances via the item veto, accountability, local autonomy). Philconsa and LAMP abandoned on this point.
        4. Belgica (2019): lump sums are not automatically pork; valid if they meet singular correspondence or have adequate standards.
        • Belgica (2013) key phrases: the PDAF was a ‘budget within a budget’ (an intermediate appropriation completed by legislators after enactment); identification was not merely recommendatory, since the fund could not be used without it; after enactment Congress’s role is limited to oversight (scrutiny and investigation).
        • LAMP failed for want of proof: speculation and media reports do not overcome the presumptions of constitutionality and regularity. Belgica held it no bar, since it decided nothing on the merits.
        • Presidential discretionary funds are not per se invalid but must meet valid-delegation standards: Belgica voided the catch-all phrases in the Malampaya Fund and Presidential Social Fund decrees.
        Singular correspondence (Belgica 2013; 2019)
        1. A valid item allocates a specified amount for a specified purpose, so the President can veto it as a unit.
        2. A lump sum is valid if all the programs, projects or activities it funds fall under one singular purpose, however general, so long as that purpose does not negate the President’s item veto (no multiple, unrelated, vague or amorphous purposes) (Belgica 2019).
        3. Invalid: a lump sum for several purposes where the amounts and projects are chosen after enactment (especially by legislators).
        Item veto and riders (Philconsa v. Enriquez)
        1. An item is an indivisible sum of money for a stated purpose; the President vetoes it whole or not at all.
        2. A provision that does not relate to a particular appropriation, or that amends substantive law, is an ‘inappropriate provision’ (rider) and may be vetoed as if it were an item.
        3. An appropriate provision or condition can be struck only by vetoing the item it qualifies. So the vetoes of the debt service restriction, the DPWH 70/30 road-maintenance rule and the AFP medicine-purchase provision were void.

        Transfers, savings and augmentation

        Art. VI, Sec. 25(5) requisites (Demetria; Araullo)
        1. A law (usually the GAA) authorizes the officer to augment.
        2. There are actual savings: the purpose was completed or abandoned, or efficiencies achieved, after the item was fully provided for. Unreleased or unobligated funds declared ‘savings’ mid-year are not savings.
        3. The transfer augments an existing item in the GAA (not a new project with no appropriation).
        4. The transfer stays within the officer’s own branch or office (no ‘cross-border’ transfers).
        • Demetria v. Alba (1987): a blanket authority to transfer any fund to any project is void.
        • Araullo (2014): DAP partly void (withdrawn allotments as ‘savings’; cross-border transfers; unprogrammed funds without excess revenue; projects with no appropriation). Operative fact for projects done, not for authors absent findings of good faith.
        • Pichay (2012): the President may reorganize his own office and realign its funds under the GAA.
        • Nazareth v. Villar (2013): a benefits law without an appropriation cannot be paid; savings cannot augment a non-existent item.
        • Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023): a law postponing elections to free election funds for other uses was a disguised transfer of appropriations and void.
        • Dela Cruz v. Ochoa (2018): an item for a major final output covers its integral components.
        • Madera (2020): who refunds disallowed amounts (good-faith officers do not; recipients generally do, subject to exceptions).
        • Return rules (Madera): (a) disallowance set aside: no one returns; (b) approving and certifying officers in good faith, in the regular performance of duties and with diligence: not liable; in bad faith, malice or gross negligence: solidarily liable for the net disallowed amount; (c) payees return what they received (solutio indebiti), even in good faith, unless it was genuinely for services rendered or the Court excuses it (undue prejudice, social justice, other bona fide exceptions). Badges of good faith: certificate of availability of funds, a legal opinion, no contrary precedent, long agency practice without prior disallowance, a reasonable reading of the law.
        • Guingona v. Carague (1991): automatic appropriations for debt service are valid; education’s ‘highest priority’ does not bar them.
        In a news question: (1) Confidential and intelligence funds (2016 midterm; the OVP controversy): they must be appropriated by law for a specific office and purpose; transferring them to another office mid-year is a transfer of appropriations; the Senate may delete or reduce them (Congress may decrease, never increase, the President’s recommendations); they remain subject to COA audit. (2) A GAA provision defunding a unit (2020 finals, PAO forensic lab): a condition that relates to the agency’s appropriation is not a rider; Congress may refuse to fund. A provision amending other laws or the agency’s structure is an inappropriate provision (Philconsa) that the President may veto. (3) A GAA provision letting DBM change agencies’ organizational structures: substantive legislation in a budget law relates to no particular appropriation and is a rider under Sec. 25(2).
        Traps: (1) Congress may reduce or delete but may not increase the President’s recommended appropriations for the operation of government (Sec. 25(1)). (2) The re-enacted budget applies automatically if no GAA passes (Sec. 25(7)). (3) The President’s item veto applies only to appropriation, revenue and tariff bills; elsewhere the veto is all-or-nothing.

        Taxation

        Art. VI, Sec. 28(1) The rule of taxation shall be uniform and equitable. The Congress shall evolve a progressive system of taxation. (2) The Congress may, by law, authorize the President to fix within specified limits, and subject to such limitations and restrictions as it may impose, tariff rates, import and export quotas, tonnage and wharfage dues, and other duties or imposts within the framework of the national development program of the Government. (3) Charitable institutions, churches and parsonages or convents appurtenant thereto, mosques, non-profit cemeteries, and all lands, buildings, and improvements, actually, directly, and exclusively used for religious, charitable, or educational purposes shall be exempt from taxation. (4) No law granting any tax exemption shall be passed without the concurrence of a majority of all the Members of the Congress.
        • Origination (Tolentino v. Sec. of Finance): the bill, not the law, must originate in the House; the Senate may propose amendments, even a substitute. The bicameral committee may add germane provisions. A presidential certification of urgency dispenses with both three separate readings and printing three days before.
        • Why the House: district representatives are closer to local needs; senators, elected at large, bring the national view. The Senate may file a substitute bill in anticipation of the House bill, so long as it withholds action as a body until the House bill arrives; the conference committee may add entirely new provisions found in neither version, if germane (Tolentino).
        • Uniformity and equity: taxes on persons and things of the same class at the same rate; reasonable classification allowed. The progressive taxation clause is a directive, not an enforceable right (Tolentino).
        • Valid classification (Tan v. Del Rosario): (1) rests on substantial distinctions; (2) germane to the purpose of the law; (3) not limited to existing conditions only; (4) applies equally to all members of the same class.
        • Exemptions: only Congress grants them, by a majority of all Members, expressly (John Hay PAC: no exemption by presidential proclamation). Constitutional exemption for charitable property requires actual, direct and exclusive use; leased commercial portions are taxable (Lung Center).
        • Charitable character (Lung Center): an institution is charitable if it exists for a purpose recognized in law as charitable rather than for gain or private advantage; charging paying patients and receiving subsidies do not defeat it. But the exemption follows the use of the property, not of the income, and is strictly construed against the claimant, who bears the burden of proof. Besides Congress, only the Constitution itself grants exemptions; local governments may exempt only from local taxes (John Hay).
        • Tariff delegation: valid within limits Congress sets (Garcia v. Executive Secretary).
        • A tariff measure is not invalid because it is mainly meant to raise revenue; the President, acting under Sec. 401 of the Tariff and Customs Code (national economy, general welfare, national security), is not limited to protecting local industries (Garcia).
        2015 midterm (income tax reform pushed by the House, opposed by the President): a revenue bill must originate in the House, which it did. The President’s objections are relevant only when the bill reaches him: he may then veto it (or particular items, since it is a revenue bill), and Congress may override by two-thirds of all members of each House.

        Last-minute checklist

        • Sec. 24 origination list; Senate may propose amendments (Tolentino).
        • Sec. 25(1) no increase; (2) no riders; (5) augmentation requisites; (7) re-enacted budget; Sec. 29(1) no payment without appropriation.
        • Pork line: Philconsa → LAMP → Belgica 2013 (reversal) → Belgica 2019 (lump sums can be valid).
        • Savings definition; cross-border transfers void (Araullo); Macalintal 2023 (disguised transfer).
        • Tax exemptions: majority of all members; express; not by proclamation (John Hay); actual, direct and exclusive use (Lung Center).

        2026 news watch

        Gatmaytan builds his questions from recent news (‘the stories may have been altered’). These are the stories from April to October 2026 that map onto your coverage, with the rule each one triggers. Each has a practice essay in the Essay trainer. Facts are as reported up to October 8, 2026; pending cases may move before the exam.

        Political dynasties: the Court orders Congress to legislate

        Kapatiran Party v. Congress (decision dated Aug. 26, 2026; released Sept. 16): Art. II, Sec. 26 is a mandatory command; 39 years of inaction is grave abuse; mandamus granted (by majority); Congress defines ‘political dynasty’; COMELEC cannot disqualify without the law. After the ruling, the Senate moved to seek an urgent certification for its bill (SB 1901, second-degree ban, pending on second reading); the House had passed HB 8389 on June 3.

        • Rules it triggers: self-executing provisions (Manila Prince; Art. II generally not enforceable); expanded judicial review of inaction; separation of powers (can the Court compel Congress?); and, for any dynasty law, whether a ban adds qualifications to constitutional offices (Sec. 26 is the constitutional source, unlike SJS v. DDB).
        • Practice: evaluate a senator’s critique; challenge to a dynasty law.

        VP Sara Duterte’s impeachment: who counts as ‘all the Members’?

        The House impeached the Vice President a second time on May 11, 2026 (257 votes). On September 23, the Senate impeachment court ruled 13–1 that ‘all the Members of the Senate’ (Art. XI, Sec. 3(6)) counts only senators legally and actually able to take part, excluding those detained, in hiding or incapacitated. On September 30, the Supreme Court dismissed three citizens’ petitions on procedural grounds (standing, prematurity). The trial pauses after October 15 for the 2027 budget.

        • Rules it triggers: verba legis and the deliberate contrast between ‘Members present’ and ‘all the Members’; quorum and coercive jurisdiction (Avelino); a detained member is still a member (Jalosjos); ripeness and standing; Francisco’s limits on the political question doctrine.
        • Practice: the two-thirds count.
        Coverage: impeachment (Art. XI) is not in your midterm syllabus. Use the story for interpretation, judicial review and quorum, not for impeachment procedure.

        Sen. dela Rosa, the ICC warrant and ‘protective custody’

        Absent since November 2025, Sen. Ronald dela Rosa appeared on May 11, 2026 (the day the ICC unsealed its warrant for the crime against humanity of murder) and voted to elect Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano as Senate President, 13–9–2. When NBI agents tried to arrest him in the Senate, the chamber placed him under ‘protective custody’; he left on May 14. Sen. Sherwin Gatchalian has been Senate President since June 17, 2026.

        • Rules it triggers: privilege from arrest (Sec. 11: not more than six years, while in session); Jalosjos and Trillanes; the Senate’s powers under Sec. 16 (officers by majority of all Members, quorum, compelling attendance, discipline), none of which includes shielding a member from law enforcement.
        • Practice: immunity and the Senate’s actions.

        Barangay and SK elections moved to 2028 (RA 12326)

        Signed September 24, 2026: the November 2, 2026 BSKE moves to November 2028, with five-year terms; Sec. 5 speaks of the ‘extension of their terms’. Atty. Macalintal’s petition (one-subject rule, legislative appointment, ‘endless extensions’) is pending; the OSG says the term of barangay officials is a political question.

        • Rules it triggers: the postponement guidelines in Macalintal v. COMELEC (2023): postponement is the exception; it needs important, substantial or compelling reasons; election fatigue and divisiveness are not enough; intervals must not be unduly long; it must be narrowly tailored. Also hold-over (tenure) versus term extension, and the title rule (Giron).
        • Practice: resolve the petition.

        The budget: unprogrammed funds and the PhilHealth ruling

        Reps. Erice and De Lima challenge the ₱150.9-billion unprogrammed appropriations in the 2026 GAA; the Court heard oral arguments in April with petitions on the 2024 and 2025 budgets and asked for memoranda in July. The President’s 2027 budget (₱7.2 trillion, submitted in August) cuts unprogrammed appropriations to about ₱112 billion. In Pimentel v. House (Dec. 3, 2025), the Court voided the 2024 GAA provision that swept ₱60 billion of PhilHealth funds to the Treasury.

        • Rules it triggers: Sec. 25(1) (no congressional increase), 25(2) (riders), 25(5) (augmentation by the President only, from savings), 29(3) (special funds); Belgica 2019 (standby funds valid with standards); Araullo (excess-revenue certification); the GAA cannot amend substantive law.
        • Practice: unprogrammed appropriations; a 2027 fund sweep.

        Last-minute checklist

        • Kapatiran: duty vs content vs enforcement.
        • ‘All the Members’ vs ‘Members present’; Avelino is about quorum.
        • Arrest privilege: six years and in session; the Senate cannot grant custody.
        • Election postponements: Macalintal 2023 guidelines.
        • Budget: no increase, no riders, no transfers, special funds stay special.
